title: Extraction and workup
calcLabel: Read the workup and phase separation guide

steps.q: Partition coefficient 4 (organic over water), one extraction, equal volumes. How much is extracted?
steps.title: Partition coefficient
steps.summary: The partition coefficient K is the product's concentration in the organic layer divided by its concentration in the water. With K = 4 and equal volumes the product splits four parts to one, so 4 ÷ 5 = 80 % is extracted in one pass. In general the fraction extracted is KR ÷ (1 + KR), where R is organic volume over water volume.

steps.q: Same K of 4. Is one extraction with the full solvent better, or two with half each?
steps.title: Split the solvent
steps.summary: With K = 4, one extraction with the full solvent volume leaves 1/(1+4) = 20 % behind. With half the volume each pass leaves 1/(1+2) = 1/3, so two passes leave 1/9, about 11 %, extracting about 89 %. Several smaller extractions always beat one large one, though two or three passes are usually enough in practice.

steps.q: A stubborn emulsion forms after a wash. What is a good first fix?

steps.title: Emulsions
steps.summary: An emulsion is fine droplets that will not settle, often caused by fine solids, surfactant-like by-products or too much stirring. Adding brine raises the water layer's density and ionic strength so droplets coalesce. Other fixes are time, gentle warming (well below the solvent's boiling point), adjusting pH or filtering out stabilising solids; gentler stirring prevents it.

opts.t: Add more of the same water

steps.q: An acid product (pKa 4.5) must move into the water layer. Roughly what pH should the water be?
steps.title: pH swing
steps.summary: An acid is mostly neutral below its pKa and ionised above it. Two pH units above the pKa (here pH 6.5 or higher) about 99 % is ionised and moves into water; two units below (about pH 2.5) it is neutral and stays in the organic layer. Extract the acid into water at high pH, separate, then acidify to recover it; bases behave the other way round.

steps.q: Dichloromethane (DCM) and water in a separator. Which layer is on top?
steps.title: Which way up?
steps.summary: Density decides which layer is on top. Water is 1.0 and dichloromethane about 1.33, so DCM sinks and water floats; toluene (0.87) and ethyl acetate (0.90) float on water. Salty water layers are heavier than expected and close densities can invert layers, so when in doubt, add a few drops of water to a sample and see which layer grows.

draw: test a sample: add water drops

steps.q: In the plant separator, a hazy rag layer sits between the two phases. What do you do with it?
board: What do you do with it?
steps.title: The rag layer
steps.summary: A rag layer at the interface holds fine solids, emulsion and impurities, and often some product. Drain the bottom layer slowly while watching the sight glass, stop at the rag, and take it as a separate cut to settle, filter or rework as the approved procedure allows. Drain flammable solvents slowly with the vessel and container earthed.

opts.t: Send it with the product layer
Take it as a separate cut to rework

intro.text: Hi, I'm Bubbles. Today: workup. Two liquids that won't mix, and a product that has to pick a side. Six questions. Ready?

outro-web.text: That's the lesson. Read the workup and phase separation guide next.

q1.text: Question 1. Partition coefficient 4 (organic over water), one extraction, equal volumes. How much is extracted?

q1-r0.text: 25 is one over four. The organic holds four parts out of five.

q1-r2.text: 100? Some always stays in the water.

q1-r3.text: Not quite. Work out the split between the two layers.

q1-b0.text: K is the concentration in the organic layer divided by the concentration in the water.

q1-b1.text: With equal volumes, the product splits four parts to one.

q1-b2.text: Four out of five parts is 80 percent in the organic. 20 percent stays in the water.

q1-b3.text: In general, fraction extracted is K times the volume ratio over one plus that.

q2.text: Question 2. Same K of 4. Is one extraction with the full solvent better, or two with half each?

q2-r0.text: One big wash gets 80 percent. Two halves beat it.

q2-r1.text: Two halves win: about 89 percent against 80.

q2-r2.text: Same solvent, different result. Split it.

q2-r3.text: Longer stirring helps reach balance, but the split still favours two washes.

q2-b0.text: One extraction with the full volume leaves 1 over 5 behind: 20 percent.

q2-b1.text: With half the volume, each extraction leaves 1 over 3 behind.

q2-b2.text: Two of them leave one third of one third: one ninth, about 11 percent. So about 89 percent extracted.

q2-b3.text: More, smaller extractions always beat one big one. But each extra step costs time and handling, so two or three is usually enough.

q3.text: Question 3. A stubborn emulsion forms after a wash. What is a good first fix?

q3-r0.text: Harder stirring makes finer droplets. That's how you got here.

q3-r1.text: Yes! Salt makes the water layer heavier and less friendly to the organic.

q3-r2.text: More water usually just makes more emulsion.

q3-r3.text: Then the next step gets an emulsion. Fix it here.

q3-b0.text: An emulsion is fine droplets that won't settle. Fine solids, soapy by-products or too much stirring cause it.

q3-b1.text: Brine raises the water layer's density and ionic strength. Droplets merge and the layers split.

q3-b2.text: Other fixes: give it time, warm it gently, well below the solvent's boiling point, adjust the pH, or filter out the fine solids that hold it.

q3-b3.text: And next time, stir gently during the wash. It's easier to prevent an emulsion than break one.

q4.text: Question 4. An acid product (pKa 4.5) must move into the water layer. Roughly what pH should the water be?

q4-r0.text: Below the pKa the acid is mostly neutral, and it stays in the organic.

q4-r1.text: At the pKa only half is ionised, and the neutral half still prefers the organic.

q4-r2.text: Correct! Two or more units above the pKa, it's ionised and loves water.

q4-r3.text: At pH 2 the acid is neutral, and it stays in the organic.

q4-b0.text: An acid like this is mostly neutral below its pKa, and ionised above it.

q4-b1.text: Two pH units above the pKa, about 99 percent is ionised. So pH 6.5 or more pulls it into the water.

q4-b2.text: Two units below, about pH 2.5, it's neutral and stays in the organic.

q4-b3.text: So wash at high pH to pull the acid out, separate, then acidify the water to get it back. Acidifying a carbonate wash gives off carbon dioxide, so add acid slowly and vent. Bases work the other way round.

q5.text: Question 5. Dichloromethane (DCM) and water in a separator. Which layer is on top?

q5-r0.text: DCM is heavier than water. It sinks.

q5-r1.text: Yes! DCM is about 1.33. Water floats on it.

q5-r2.text: DCM and water barely mix. You get two layers.

q5-b0.text: Density decides. Water is 1.0. DCM is about 1.33, so it goes to the bottom.

q5-b1.text: Toluene at 0.87 and ethyl acetate at 0.90 float on water.

q5-b2.text: Careful: a salty water layer can be heavier than you expect, and close densities can even flip the layers.

q5-b3.text: When in doubt, add a few drops of water to a sample and see which layer grows. Never guess on a plant cut.

q6.text: Question 6. In the plant separator, a hazy rag layer sits between the two phases. What do you do with it?

q6-r0.text: And carry water and junk into the next step? Risky.

q6-r1.text: Yes! Keep it apart, settle or rework it later.

q6-r2.text: It often holds product. Don't pour yield away.

q6-r3.text: It's where solids and impurities gather. Not harmless.

q6-b0.text: The rag layer holds fine solids, emulsion and impurities at the interface.

q6-b1.text: Drain the bottom layer slowly, watching the sight glass, and stop at the rag.

q6-b2.text: Take the rag into a separate container. Let it settle, filter it, or rework it as your approved procedure allows.

q6-b3.text: Drain flammable solvents slowly, with the vessel and container earthed. More in the workup guide on pharmacheme dot in.
